front: Why do the dynamics vanish from the gradient?
back: $\log p_\theta(\tau)=\sum\log\pi_\theta+\text{terms independent of }\theta$, so only the policy terms are differentiated.
Weight $\nabla\log\pi(a_t|s_t)$ by $G_t$ (future rewards) rather than the whole return; same expectation, lower variance.

front: Why a state baseline is unbiased

back: $A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)$: how much better an action is than the policy's average in that state.
Actor: the policy $\pi_\theta$. Critic: a value estimate $V_\phi(s)$ that provides the baseline/advantage.
TD: $r+\gamma V(s')-V(s)$, low variance, biased. MC: $G_t-V(s_t)$, unbiased, high variance.
Synchronous advantage actor-critic: parallel rollouts, advantage estimates, one actor and one critic step on the batch, usually plus an entropy bonus.
$-\text{adv}\cdot\log\pi_\theta(a|s)$ with the advantage detached (a constant weight).

front: Main weakness of vanilla policy gradients
back: High variance and on-policy data: each batch supports roughly one gradient step.
$+c_eH(\pi_\theta)$ discourages premature collapse to a deterministic policy and keeps exploring.
